speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43. Whereas the port of Churchill is an economic benefit to many farmers who wish to ship their grain through Churchill and that under the existing disastrous mismanagement only 300,000 tonnes were shipped through Churchill this year, and since the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) has refused to set up a separate committee to study the improved use of Churchill for shipment of grains and other products, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Lewycky):
That this House instruct the Minister of Transport to establish immediately a committee that will make recommendations to improve grain transportation through Churchill for next year, and that this same committee will be asked to make recommendations for the expanded use of the port in the future.

That this House takes note of repeated commitments to equal rights for women, and therefore calls on the government to act on these commitments in terms of job opportunities and equal pay for work of equal value, as well as in providing pension coverage on a universal basis, equivalent to the Canada Pension Plan, for women who work in their homes, and also by eliminating forthwith the discrimination against women between 60 and 65 who are without spouses, it being the view of this House that all women in that age bracket should be entitled to the equivalent of the spouse's allowance, regardless of marital status.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, because of the importance of this matter for the future of many young Canadians I have some grounds for hope that this House will give unanimous consent to my urgent and pressing motion under Standing Order 43.
Because of the damage to mental and physical health caused by the ingestion of the hallucinogenic so-called "magic mushrooms" now coming to maturity and being harvested in large quantities on Vancouver Island and in the Fraser Valley, and in view of the legal difficulties confronting the police and farm owners to control the situation because these hallucinogens are not considered prohibited items under the Food and Drugs Act, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Fraser Valley West (Mr. Wenman):

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise under the authority of Standing Order 43. Whereas section 101 of the Criminal Code of Canada allows a police officer to search a person's home without a warrant and to seize any firearm when no crime has been committed and no charge has been laid, whereas a judge has ruled that this section is ultra vires and that the implications of this section are "frightening", and whereas such searches and seizures are contrary to the Canadian Bill of Rights, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Towers):

As reported in Hansard for May 22 at page 1305, the Metric Commission has already spent over $25 million promoting the metric methodology, and $27 million more have been earmarked for the next three fiscal years. INQUIRY RESPECTING JUICE APPLE SURPLUS IN ONTARIO
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Agriculture. According to the minister's departmental officials the minister has refused to help the Apple Marketing Commission deal with the 5,000-ton juice apple surplus which exists in Ontario. Can the minister tell the House, firstly, why he refused; and, second, in light of the fact that for most of the smaller apple farmers this loss represents the loss of primary income, not secondary income as the department would have us believe, why would he not offer the same assistance to the apple farmers as he has to the cherry and grape growers?

speakeroldname: Hon. E. F. Whelan (Minister of Agriculture):
subtopic: INQUIRY RESPECTING JUICE APPLE SURPLUS IN ONTARIO
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the answer is quite clear. There is no place to put the apples. There is nothing to be done with them. There is no method of processing we can find which can process them into juice or other alternatives, according to the information I have.
I understand some of these apples are being moved into other markets in Quebec and Nova Scotia where the apple crop is not as heavy.
The information I have is contrary to what the member gives the House and myself. These apples are secondary apples, apples which have fallen and are bruised. They normally go into cider and there are 5,000 tons that they want me to buy. If the member can find a place where they can be processed I will reconsider the decision I made, but I just cannot see buying apples and dumping them on the ground.

subtopic: INQUIRY RESPECTING JUICE APPLE SURPLUS IN ONTARIO
speechtext: Madam Speaker, would the minister tell the House why he is allowing so much concentrate to be dumped into Canada from countries such as Chile, Argentina and South Africa? Approximately 17.98 million pounds were dumped in 1979, and this has a serious effect on our domestic industry.

subtopic: INQUIRY RESPECTING JUICE APPLE SURPLUS IN ONTARIO
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, if the hon. member can find a healthier industry in the entire horticultural industry than the apple industry, I would like him to tell me. The apple industry has had a very good year economically. There is a very good apple marketing commission in Ontario. The tremendous crop this year will benefit the entire industry.
Also, the government has given the industry assistance up to one-third of the cost of storage, up to $500,000 for controlled atmospheric temperature storage. There is more storage now than ever before for all Canadian apples. For instance, this year British Columbia is exporting apples to approximately 40 different countries around the world, and this is because of the programs which we have initiated. Naturally, sometimes we take in produce from other parts of the world.

subsubtopic: INVESTMENT TAX CREDIT-ALLEGED DISCRIMINATORY APPLICATION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of National Revenue. It is with regard to the very serious discrimination which exists in the area of taxation on equipment used to haul wood-converting products, particularly logs. As the minister knows, there is an investment tax credit for such equipment as it applies to larger companies, but private trucking loggers-in other words, small independent operators-are not benefiting from the investment tax credit. The minister is aware of this fact because he has been dealing with the problem since he became the minister and it has been referred to the department before.
Why does this anomaly exist and what does the minister intend to do about it? When can we expect the necessary changes which will remove this discrimination against private operators?

subsubtopic: INVESTMENT TAX CREDIT-ALLEGED DISCRIMINATORY APPLICATION
speechtext: Madam Speaker, generally speaking the people who haul the logs are not connected with the forest products industry, and we make that distinction. However, the situation is under review at the present time. 1 am taking a look at the situation to determine if we can accommodate the small businessmen who haul the logs, but generally speaking it is the lack of integration with the forest products industry which creates the problem.

subsubtopic: INVESTMENT TAX CREDIT-ALLEGED DISCRIMINATORY APPLICATION

subtopic: CANADA SAVINGS BONDS-INQUIRY WHETHER INTEREST RATE WILL BE INCREASED

Will the minister at this point increase the rate paid on Canada Savings Bonds to be more in step with the rate he pays the big banks and financial institutions for treasury bills and bonds so that the ordinary people will have at least a rate of return on their bonds equal to, or better than, the rate of inflation?

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
subtopic: CANADA SAVINGS BONDS-INQUIRY WHETHER INTEREST RATE WILL BE INCREASED
speechtext: Madam Speaker, 1 will give careful consideration to the hon. member's suggestion that 1 should increase the rate of return on Canada Savings Bonds, despite the fact that at the present time it is a very attractive investment; it is high quality and can be cashed at any time. Quite apart from these positive features, however, 1 will consider what he has to suggest.

subtopic: CANADA SAVINGS BONDS-INQUIRY WHETHER INTEREST RATE WILL BE INCREASED
speechtext:
A supplementary question, Madam Speaker. If the minister is going to do that, I think a rate of at least 11.5 per cent would be appropriate. On this side of the House we know the cost of selling bonds, we know the redeeming features of them and all the rest. The minister would not even be paying a rate equal to the 90-day treasury bill rate, which is essentially an instant cash instrument, if he increased the rate on those bonds to 11.5 per cent.
Would the minister give the House a commitment that, before the time limit for the sale of the bonds expires, he will be fair to the people who have bought them and will stand behind his advertising which indicates that they are a good deal, when in fact he knows they are not?

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
subtopic: CANADA SAVINGS BONDS-INQUIRY WHETHER INTEREST RATE WILL BE INCREASED
speechtext: Madam Speaker, when we set the rate for Canada Savings Bonds our objective was not only to make the bonds attractive for prospective purchasers but also to reduce to the lowest possible amount the burden on the public treasury. My hon. friend knows that even a 1 per cent increase in the rate of return involves a very substantial increased burden upon the treasury and upon future payments on the national debt. It was in order to reduce that impact as much as possible, and at the same time to provide for a sale, that we set the rate at 10.5 per cent. subsubtopic: DORCHESTER, N.B.-INQUIRY AS TO PROGRESS OF INVESTIGATION INTO CONDITIONS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, as I indicated to the House earlier, three inquiries into this matter are under way. One is being conducted by the RCMP under the provincial contract. That has resulted in charges being laid and I understand that investigation may be continuing. There is another, the special inquiry being conducted by the inspector general's division within the correctional service of Canada, to which had been added, for the first time that I am aware of, an independent outsider to sit as one of the inquiring officers. 1 will receive that report in the next day or two and, of course, will look at it with great interest to make sure that the recommendations contained in it for improving the security for the institution are implemented. Third, the independent provincial coroner of New Brunswick has indicated that he will be conducting a public inquest in the latter half of November into the death and into the circumstances surrounding it.
In view of all of those inquiries, I do not think that for the time being any statement of facts or official version of facts coming from me would be helpful or that any further action by way of inquiry would be justified until the results of these three investigations or inquiries are available.

To our mind, it is imperative that the gas pipeline be extended to the Maritimes without any delay, as quickly as possible, to reduce the dependence of those provinces on oil imports. speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in answer to his question, I should like to point out to the Leader of the Opposition that our constitutional endeavour entails a proposed resolution that will be studied by a committee of the House in coming days. speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Madam Speaker, when ten o'clock was called last Thursday evening I was in the process of saying that the 32-cent a gallon increase for gasoline, which would have affected Canadians by the end of this year under the Tory budget of 1979, is a far cry from the 13.3-cent a gallon increase which will affect consumers with our government's budget.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is nonsense.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
To continue, hon. members opposite who predicted that this government would deindex personal income tax were also proved wrong. This government and this Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) realized that to do away with indexing of personal income taxes would adversely affect the low and middle-income wage earners in Canada.
It is not now, nor has it ever been the intent of the Liberal government to have the little guy bear the brunt of providing
The Budget-Mr. Henderson
the necessary revenues to ensure the economic viability of this country. The government did not intend to overburden poor Canadians from every province in this country. Make no mistake about it, there are many poor Canadians in the western provinces. Not everyone in the western provinces owns his own home or drives a big car or, indeed, has a summer cottage.
This government will look for the necessary revenue where the money is, in excess of oil and gas industry profits. It will collect additional taxes from the oil and gas industry. This does not seem unrealistic to me nor to a great many other Canadians. A number of members, including myself, when speaking of the constitution, have said that Canadians by their very nature are willing to share. This willingness to share is one of the traits in true Canadians which is to be admired. If this great country of ours, this Canada, is to continue to grow and prosper from sea to sea, I believe that willingness to share must be evident from sea to sea.
In the interests of the social and economic well-being of all Canadians, but more important of poor Canadians, and in the interests of the national unity of this great country, we must all be prepared to share. Every province in this country throughout our history at one point in time has required the understanding, compassion, and assistance of other provinces. This is a fact which no doubt will be a reality for the next 113 years of our history.
Many positive steps have been taken by my hon. colleague, the Minister of Finance, which will have a beneficial effect on the national scene, but I would like to comment, if I may, on some of the more positive steps taken to alleviate regional disparity or, perhaps to be a little more specific, disparity in Atlantic Canada and, in particular, my province of Prince Edward Island.
The extension of the natural gas pipeline system to Quebec City and the maritimes is very welcome news indeed. Portions of Quebec and the provinces of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia being afforded the opportunity to switch from oil to natural gas will lessen the dependency of the Atlantic region on offshore oil. This offshore oil that the Atlantic region must depend on is unreliable at this point in time, and continues to escalate in price.
The fund which will support the conversion of the Atlantic region's oil-fired electrical plants to coal will have a direct and very positive effect. A positive impact on my province of Prince Edward Island, because its requirement is totally electrical energy from oil-fired plants, will also be felt. A consequence of this requirement is that Prince Edward Island has the highest electrical rates of any province in Canada. I speak of provinces. I realize that the Northwest Territories and Yukon probably had, and have, higher oil prices.
This government, realizing that neither Newfoundland nor Prince Edward Island have access to western natural gas, has initiated a program which provides for a major housing retrofit program which includes energy audits, oil furnace retrofits,

November 3, 1980
The Budget-Mr. Henderson
and additional insulation. This grant will cover 50 per cent of the costs involved, up to a maximum of $800. That is the cost of the retrofits. This program will also be made available in the Yukon and Northwest Territories. I was pleased that the Prince Edward Island conservation and renewable energy agreement will be extended. The four-year cost of this conservation and renewable energy agreement will be $9 million.
The special emphasis on renewables development in Prince Edward Island, where alternate energies are concerned, reflect the support given to conservation and renewable energies by public action and public policy in my province. In fact, my province is considered to be leading the way in Canada in research of renewable energies.
I am also extremely pleased that the 9 per cent excise tax on the packaging of farm produce will be removed as of January 1, 1981. This was, of course, very welcome news for the potato producers of Prince Edward Island. I had considerable communication about this tax with the hon. Minister of Finance, and obviously the minister has listened and responded not only to the farmers of Prince Edward Island but also, indeed, to farmers right across the country.
Another very important announcement in the budget which affects my constituency perhaps to a greater extent than others was the full indexing of personal income taxes for 1981. In my constituency there is a large percentage of low and middle-income families, and they very definitely would have felt the full effect of any de-indexing program. The rationale used by the Minister of Finance was sound indeed.
Indexing of personal income tax ensures that increases in income which just keep pace with inflation will not force higher income tax burdens on low-income people. Certainly of major importance is that low and middle-income families will receive the refundable tax child credit. The indexing of that child tax credit ensures that its real value to families is maintained.
Opposition members have been quoted as saying that this budget does nothing for the unemployment situation facing Canada. The investment tax credits for new capital investments made in selective regions is being increased from its present 20 per cent maximum rate to 50 per cent in selected regions. These selected regions will be determined on the basis of criteria such as high unemployment and low income levels. Again I say that we should be trying to attract business in areas where there are low income levels. By attracting industries to these regions, quite obviously jobs will be created and fewer people will be unemployed.
I suggest also that the reintroduction of the MURB program will provide a stimulus to the construction industry which will provide employment for large numbers of qualified workers in the construction trades.
Further, the energy policy of this government, if analysed with some degree of intelligence, indicates vast potential for job creation. As a matter of fact this energy policy could, I believe, be accurately described as a job creation energy policy. Just one of the many projects outlined in our energy
policy is the extension of the natural gas pipeline to the maritimes.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Don't hold your breath.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Does the hon. member over there believe that a project of this magnitude would require any less than thousands of workers not only in the manufacturing of the pipe but also the laying of the pipe and so forth? A project of this magnitude would produce obvious spin-off effects. This is fact.
This government has reserved $350 million for manpower retraining programs. As hon. members know, there is a large number of people who lack the necessary skills to enter a very competitive labour force. This $350 million will finance manpower retraining programs which will provide people all over the country with marketable skills. It would appear to me that members of the opposition, because their own budget sank with their Jolly Roger, Captain Crosbie, are now grasping at straws and trying desperately to create troubled waters for this government's budget. I can assure hon. members opposite that this budget will not sink. It will steam straight ahead, and Canadians from one coast to the other will enjoy the benefits from it.
In my opening remarks I made reference to the increase of 32 cents a gallon on gasoline in the Crosbie budget of December of last year. I compared that with the 13.3 cents in my colleague's budget. Perhaps we can carry that comparison just a little further. By the end of 1981 the cost of a gallon of gasoline at the pumps in Toronto, with this government's budget, will be $1.36. The Conservative budget of 1979 would have meant a price at the pump in Toronto of $ 1.56 a gallon, a difference of 20 cents a gallon.
By the end of 1982, again using Toronto as a mean average, the government's budget will mean $1.53 a gallon at the pumps, while the Conservative budget of 1979 would mean $1.75 a gallon, or a difference of 22 cents a gallon.
As we go on, the comparison becomes even more dramatic, Mr. Speaker. By the end of 1983 our budget will mean that the cost of a gallon of gasoline at the pump in Toronto will be $1.71 a gallon. The ill-fated Tory budget of 1979 would mean we would be paying $2.32 a gallon, or a difference of 61 cents a gallon.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, because I know hon. members opposite are becoming somewhat embarrassed-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
While I am comparing the relative costs of gasoline under the budget presented by the hon. member for St. John's West and that of my colleague, the Minister of Finance, I believe it would be appropriate to respond to statements made to the effect that this budget has nothing in it for the farmers and fishermen in this country. This is one of the statements which has been made. It seems ironic that the hon. member for St. John's West should make such a statement, because it was the farmers and fishermen in my riding who could have least afforded the very dramatic forecasted rapid increases in the cost of gasoline suggested by the hon. gentleman opposite.
We have heard statements from the other side of the House about the flight of the wild geese, the plucking of the goose with its wings flapping, and so on. Well, Mr. Speaker, the ill-fated budget of December 11, 1979, the Christmas budget which was brought down just 14 days, not 12 days, before Christmas, was 1 submit, a turkey budget, a budget which would have had my farmers and fishermen in Prince Edward Island flocking from the sea and the land like a flock of turkeys. I believe that almost every one can live with and benefit from this government's budget. The farmers and the fishermen will feel the effects of this budget because it is designed to ensure the economic stability of this country.
We have also heard from hon. members on the other side of the House statements to the effect that members on this side of the House do not understand the west. I think there is a need for a better understanding of all parts of Canada by all of us in the House, and indeed not only but us in this House but by all Canadians. When I was last out west I heard statements to the effect that we were probably not aware of what was going on out there. But when I got a little deeper into the conversation I found that when they were talking about the east they meant mainly Montreal and Toronto.
When I explained to them-these were mainly working people-that there are four provinces east of Montreal, they began to think and to understand a little bit better what the east really is. When I told them that we in the maritimes rely on industries such as agriculture, fisheries, tourism, small business, and so on, all of them high energy consuming industries, they understood immediately why we could not take rapid increases in oil prices. I believe that is very, very important, because a country can be compared to a chain-it is only as strong as its weakest link. Therefore, if we are to have a strong country, we have to grow and develop together and we have to look after one and other, as provinces have over the last number of years.
When confederation was formed, Atlantic Canada was composed of the "have" provinces, but then the emphasis shifted to
The Budget-Mr. Wilson
central Canada. Of course now, undoubtedly, the emphasis is shifting to western Canada. We must keep this country united and we must ensure that, by allowing a rapid increase in the wealth of one area, we will not allow another area to deteriorate. I submit that we must not allow this to happen.
Before my time runs out, Mr. Speaker, I should like to comment briefly on the government's objectives to achieve at least 50 per cent Canadian ownership of the oil and gas industries by 1990. I have had a number of comments from my constituents in this regard and I have found that, without exception, the general feeling is that natural resources in Canada should be owned and controlled by Canadians. I submit that this general feeling is felt right across this country in all constituencies.
I know that my time is up, Mr. Speaker, so in conclusion I should like to congratulate once again my colleague, the Minister of Finance, for presenting a budget which 1 think is as fair and equitable to Canadians as we could expect in such difficult times experienced not only in this country but, indeed, in the world.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the debate today on the budget and the energy statement of last Tuesday is one of the most important we have seen and will see in the irhirty-second Parliament. It is very significant that it should have followed so soon after the historic debate on the constitutional resolution. The energy policy sets out in very real terms that we have been debating in somewhat abstract terms in the constitutional debate. It shows vividly how, in its greedy and self-centred view of Canada, the federal government is attempting to capture significantly greater power and ever-increasing tax dollars in a unilateral way without regard for the history and the constitutional position of the regions of this country.
The constitutional proposals of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) would allow the federal government to bypass the legislatures of Canada. The energy proposals show clearly how it would do so. The objectives of the energy proposals show clearly how it would do so. The objectives of the energy proposals are very noble in intent, but the means to achieve these objectives as laid out in the national program are incompatible with the over-all objectives.
As we have said on many occasions, self-sufficiency should be our primary objective, our overriding objective in the energy policy. The precarious position of the Middle East with the current Iran-lraq war should tell us that. We should be attempting to protect ourselves from shortages in the Middle East and gain from having the increased energy dollars spent here in Canada promoting new investment, new jobs, and new technology, from which ail Canadians can benefit.
The government sets out self-sufficiency as the first objective of the energy policy, but the other two objectives, namely, revenue sharing and increasing Canadianization, totally undermine this policy objective. It was generally recognized that the Clark government energy policy could achieve energy self-sufficiency by 1990.

November 3, 1980
The Budget-Mr. Wilson

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It is doubtful whether this dog's breakfast masquerading as an energy policy with all its inconsistencies will ever achieve that important goal. It takes direct aim at the two chief partners of energy policy, the producing provinces and the industry. Canadian consumers, many in central Canada and Atlantic Canada, are being asked to pay the equivalent of $1 more for a gallon of gasoline by 1984. Huge amounts of money are being provided by consumers, but for what purpose? The consumer wants to be absolutely sure that the result will justify the cost. Will Canada achieve energy self-sufficiency by 1990? I am afraid not, Mr. Speaker.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: No way under this budget.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The Clark government proposals were costly, I will not deny that, but they had a purpose, a clear goal, namely, energy self-sufficiency. The new Liberal policy has one clear objective, not nearly so clearly stated, namely, more revenues for the federal government. It is a mammoth tax grab to pay for their profligate spending of the past 12 years.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
These words may sound somewhat familiar to Mr. Speaker. On December 11, 1979, the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gray), when he was the finance critic, said that "this Conservative energy package was really a disguised tax increase, a mammoth tax grab from the Canadian people." But let us compare the two proposals, because they are very, very different.
The Conservative budget called for an 18-cent excise tax, a 50 per cent federal share in price increases over $2 per barrel, offset by an energy tax to help those hit hardest by rising energy prices. Net revenues to the federal government for the three years ending March 31, 1984, were projected at $12.8 billion, a large figure. The Liberal budget proposes an 8 per cent production tax, an increasing natural gas excise tax, an increasing petroleum compensation charge, and a Canadian ownership charge. That will produce a monstrous $37.5 billion tax grab for the federal government, about three times "the mammoth tax grab" to which the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce objected. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Mac-Eachen) goes hunting with an elephant gun.
Let us put that into perspective because there has been some discussion about the shares taken by different levels of government. With all the increased taxes layered on each other, the cost of a barrel of oil in 1983 will be $32.80, out of which the federal government will take $17.38, or 53 per cent. The House should not let the minister fool it about the petroleum compensation charge.
In 1975 when the Hon. John Turner imposed the 10-cent excise tax on gasoline, which subsequently was reduced to 7 cents as part of an election bribe, he said that it was to offset the growing cost of imported oil. That tax followed an export tax on oil and oil products. Together these two taxes produce
today about $1.4 billion in revenue with the clear purpose of paying the oil import subsidy. But we do not hear that any more these days; it has been forgotten. It has been blended into government revenues so that now we have the compensation charge which is the only apparent tax used to offset import costs. As indicated on page 32 of the budget papers, this charge is producing even more revenue than is necessary to meet import costs-a total of $885 million in the years 1982 and 1983 more than is required to offset the cost of imports. Clearly the government is using the energy situation to increase its slice of the economic pie at the expense of the consumer. In that three-year period we will have about a $4 billion increased tax. Initially set out as being to offset the cost of imports, it will go straight into government revenues, and it is not mentioned at all by the Minister of Finance.
Also let me respond to the challenge of the Minister of Finance to my leader to show that the government has placed a greater burden on the Canadian consumer in its budget than would have been the case in the budget of the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie). In spite of claims to the contrary. Liberals have broken their campaign promise not to increase the cost of oil over $4 per barrel. The increase up until this budget was $3, there was the 75-cent Syncrude levy and now there is a further 80-cent tax as a result of the budget, for a total of $4.55, against the increase of $4 of the hon. member for St. John's West.
The increased cost of driving a car under both budgets would be about the same, but because the petroleum compensation charge and the Canadian ownership charge are very regressive and pervasive, the costs of oil heating are up by a total of $128 a year over the cost provided in the "Crosbie" budget. For low and middle-income earners the difference is almost three times that because of the energy tax credit, $337 billion a year. So much for the toothless challenge of the Minister of Finance. The burden on the consumer is clearly greater and the beneficiary is the tax department here in Ottawa, the piranha which attacks the savings of Canadian individuals.
What has happened to the industry? Why is it that oil and gas shares have dropped close to 9 per cent in the immediate aftermath of the budget? Share values are directly related to profitability, but what is profitability? Profitability is the measure of the cash flow, the money which oil companies use to pay for their exploration, development, and production activity. To most Canadians the decline in the stock market signalled a reduction in the ability of oil companies, the Canadian ones too, to find and produce oil and natural gas to free us from dependence on Middle East and other foreign producers.
The budget set out a most burdensome program to reduce cash flows. Natural gas revenues are frozen for a year; consumers will pay more but the increased amount will go to the federal treasury. Oil prices will be lower than those proposed this summer by the Prime Minister. A major portion of the industry, the 70 per cent controlled by foreign companies, will lose all conventional oil and natural gas exploration and
November 3, 1980

development incentives. These will be phased out by the end of 1983. In addition to that there will be the 8 per cent production tax.
Against this background the United States embarked upon an ambitious incentive program to reduce its dependence on imported oil. Prior to the budget of last Tuesday, that was a major incentive for drilling rigs and crews to move south of the border. That incentive has now increased markedly. Prior to the budget the U.S. netback was about $25-that is the netback to the producer-and in Canada it was about $9.70. That would have been partially offset by a windfall profits tax in the United States of about 15 per cent. But the incentive has now increased markedly to move south of the border, thus removing an important element in our battle to achieve selfsufficiency. The multinationals will not be moving south. Their territory is in Canada. The companies which will be moving capital, equipment and men into the United States will be Canadian companies, the companies the government wants to strengthen, the companies the government wants to play a bigger role in our industry.
Canadianization of the oil and gas industry is a very laudable goal. It is a goal we support and were moving toward last December. But our approach was to do it with the carrot, not the stick. Whatever we think of multinationals, we must recognize one fact: they play an important role in the oil and gas industry. They have brought the expertise, technology and capital resources which have been important elements in our success in Canada. To embark upon such an abrupt change in the rules, as proposed in the budget, will undoubtedly set back our ability to achieve the number one objective-energy selfsufficiency. The reason is that all drilling incentives for conventional oil will be phased out for companies 50 per cent or more foreign-owned by 1983. That represents 70 per cent of our industry.
There is a hidden casualty in this program-the many smaller Canadian oil and gas companies that have encountered increasing costs because of their inability to sell one of their products, natural gas. With no increase in the wellhead price for natural gas until January 1, 1982, a number of these companies will now face the prospect of selling out, perhaps but not necessarily to Petro-Canada.
We want to see more Canadian ownership in this industry, but first and foremost we want our security of supply maintained and improved. The means of achieving that Canadianization goal seem to be designed to undercut the ability of the industry to achieve security of supply. The goal seems to be to force more companies into state ownership, a nationalization of the industry.
What would be the role of Petro-Canada in this plan and what would its mandate be? Plow much of the industry will it be told to acquire? Plow much will it spend on the program? To Canadians this was previously a somewhat academic question. But now to buy out Gulf, Shell or Imperial it will cost Canadians 15 cents a gallon for a minimum of a year, and
The Budget-Mr. Wilson
most likely longer. Canadians have a right to know how much it is going to cost them, since they will be paying for it right at the pump.
The differences between the Clark government's approach to Petro-Canada and this government's approach are quite startling. The Conservative plan gave Canadians the option of participating and of directly sharing in the profits. Last year the Clark government proposed to offer Canadians shares in Petro-Canada, partially through a gift of shares and partially through the cash purchase of shares. The cash received would be used to strengthen Petro-Canada and to allow it to acquire one or more multinational oil companies, to quote our press release. The Liberal plan forces Canadians to participate and it gives them no opportunity for sharing in the profits. The Minister of Finance wants to save all that for himself.
The other major partners in achieving self-sufficiency are the producing provinces. In a unilateral, sometimes confronta-tionist, sometimes devious way, the federal government has moved to exert greater control and to extract considerably more revenues from an asset which, after all, is owned by the provinces. The response has been swift and not unexpected. The provinces of Saskatchewan and British Columbia have proposed court action to oppose the tax on natural gas and the 8 per cent production tax. Alberta has indicated its intention to extend the life of its oil reserves by cutting production by 15 per cent. Let us not forget that the established reserves of Alberta are on a clear declining trend, having declined each year for the past ten years. Alberta has also put a hold on new oil sands projects.
Who is the winner in this conflict? There is no winner-not the Alberta government, not the federal government, not the industry, which is clearly caught in the middle of a squeeze play between two levels of government. I remind you, Mr. Speaker, the last time this happened was 1973-74 when we lost a lot of ground in developing our resources in this country. And certainly the Canadian consumer is not the winner.
The province of Alberta has been a tough bargainer, which we found out last year and which the federal government has found out over the past few months. But an agreement is surely possible, as it was for us last December and should be for the federal government now. I do not see how the federal government can possibly expect Alberta to accept this policy, which is less attractive than the one offered by the Prime Minister this summer.
Since the Lougheed statement on Thursday night the government's first response was conciliatory, it was positive, and encouraging to us on this side of the House. We strongly urged the government not to escalate this conflict further and to negotiate in good faith. How then can they justify the remarks of the Minister of Finance and of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) that price is non-negotiable? It appears that the government is trying to undermine these negotiations before they get started. So the big loser is Canada-our country. There is tremendous vitality and energy in the west which can be directed to the benefit of all Canada. The Clark government had moved to harness that energy and

November 3, 1980
The Budget-Mr. Wilson
strength. This government, whether out of greed, jealousy or envy, has chosen to try to conquer that strength and to force it to submit to the will of Ottawa. That is no way to deal with a partner in confederation who can make such a powerful contribution to our future.
One of the initial responses to this policy is an almost doubling of the support for separatism in western Canada. So I ask you, Mr. Speaker, who benefits from this attack which could lead to a further division within this country?
I move to the area of economic development because there is a close link between energy policy and our economic developT ment. While the budget does promise some welcome, though small, addition to economic development funding, the energy policy may well nullify that.
Non-conventional sources of oil-mainly the major oil sands projects-are projected in the new policy to provide more oil production in 1990 than through conventional sources. These non-conventional sources will provide roughly 50 per cent of our source of supply, which is up from less than 10 per cent last year. These projects therefore are critical to our success in achieving self-sufficiency in oil. They are huge projects and require about seven years to complete. So we must move quickly to bring them onstream.
There are other reasons for moving quickly. These projects will provide tremendous economic development opportunities throughout Canada, not just in Alberta but right here in central Canada, it is estimated that about 42 per cent of the over-all economic benefit will be felt in Alberta. About 38 per cent of the activity will come to Ontario and Quebec through the purchase of steel, metal products, machinery, transportation equipment, and other manufactured goods and various services. We have all seen pictures of the huge scoops used in the Syncrude project. These scoops can now be made in Dundas, Ontario. This translates into many jobs. With an 8.7 per cent projected unemployment rate and over one million people out of work this winter, we must move quickly to bring these projects forward. For every ten people directly involved in the Alsands project it is estimated that ten more will be employed in Alberta and six more in other parts of Canada.
Consumers in other parts of Canada must understand the tremendous benefits to the whole country of these projects. If we are to be asked to pay one dollar more for a gallon of gasoline we want to receive some benefits, both in security of supply and increased economic activity. We want to bring these projects forward. But because so much of that dollar goes to the federal government-and because of its confronta-tionist tactics-the dollar is not buying us energy security or economic development.
For some years we have been concerned with the importance of developing our talents in areas where we have natural strengths. One of these areas is clearly oil sands development.
It will be a tragedy for Canada if these projects are delayed because of the tremendous opportunities there are internationally. The United States and other countries are embarked upon huge programs to upgrade refineries and bring in new energy-producing processes. The availability of process engineers, the engineers who understand how to bring these new processes into production, is critical to do this job. These people are in demand throughout the world because their skills are essential in keeping the huge costs of these megaprojects under control. A grave shortage of these skills is now a real possibility.
If these oil sands projects are delayed further, consumers in all parts of Canada will suffer in two key ways. First, the efforts to reduce our dependence on offshore oil will be delayed. Second, because of these delays we may be forced to rely on less than the best talents. The best talents will have been hired away. We stand a good chance of seeing the costs for these projects climb out of control. That happened before in 1974 and it could easily happen again. It would hit us all directly in the pocketbook.
A side effect of the delay is that other countries will develop their technology in this area faster than we do. Today we are world leaders. The Venezuelans want to involve us in the development of their giant Orinoco sands. Delays will cause them to shift to others who will have developed their skills faster than we have.
There are some nice words in the budget statement on economic development. The envelope will be increased by 22 per cent next year. But in cutting through it all, the impact is either minimal or misplaced. First, we have the western development fund, which is an attempt to buy western votes with the money the federal government has taken away in the energy tax grab. Significantly, only 50 per cent of the fund will be spent before the next election. One wonders if western Canadian voters at the next election will have a gun put to their heads-vote Liberal or risk losing the balance of the fund. Lloyd, I think you should get it in writing.
Without this fund the increases in spending for economic development in the next three years are 15 per cent, 8 per cent, and 8 per cent respectively, less than the projected inflation rate in the final two years. The result is that there is very little left for the three important areas, research and development, export promotion, and industrial expansion. One hiccup from either Chrysler or Massey-Ferguson and it is all gone. I urge the minister to get in there and fight for these worthy projects. More funding is required.
The Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce has spoken recently of his desire to increase the funding for the defence industry productivity program, DIPP, and of the need for a similar program for non-defence industries. If the money available in the economic development budget is not sufficient to provide for this, the minister will have been badly let down by his cabinet colleagues.
We on this side are also worried about the minister's ability to meet the needs of all parts of this country on such a tight budget. Canadians have many worthy social objectives, many of which have been translated into programs in recent years. We must devote much attention and funding toward our manufacturing industry which is facing major challenges in
November 3, 1980

expanding its marketplace to be able to afford those social programs. Last year Canada had a $17 billion trade deficit on manufactured products. The $175 million increase in the minister's budget is small comfort to the manufacturing community.
The real weakness of the budget, however, is that it does nothing to improve the environment for industry in Canada. Inflation will continue at a high rate. The federal budget deficit is projected at $14.2 billion, $3.6 billion higher than under our administration. Interest rates are likely to rise and the Canadian dollar will be under further downward pressure. The consensus from economists is that the budget will have a slightly negative impact on an already declining economy.
The results are obvious. Next year unemployment will soar. The rate is 8.7 per cent. Consumers will be hard hit by the increased cost of living and we will be no further ahead in developing this country's resource and labour potential. The province of Ontario has found it necessary to introduce a mini-budget to provide some stimulus to their economy, and if the energy megaprojects do not soon proceed, this sad picture will deteriorate even further. It is interesting to note that the Ontario government has the room to introduce a mini-budget because it has in recent years taken much tighter control of its own spending programs, thus it has this flexibility and the room in which to move at a time like this when such programs are really needed.
To sum up, we have a budget which adopts a stand-pat, do-nothing position. It extends the sorry state of the economy for at least another year. In those areas where there is some sign of positive initiatives, the budget proposals are, at the same time, too vague to judge, and too small to have any impact.
The main thrust of the budget statement is in the area of energy. The stated directions of the energy proposals are good, self-sufficiency, more Canadian ownership and fairness, but the means chosen to achieve these goals are contradictory, punitive and, in fact, will lead away from greater security of supply for Canadians. The proposals will result only in increased taxes to the federal government, less economic development, and to a seriously weakened partnership between Canadians across this great country.
Canadian people are being asked to provide enormous amounts of money, and they are expecting to see security of supply and economic development opportunities. But 1 am afraid to say that, when they look back in 1985 or in 1990, they will feel a great sense of frustration and anger at the result of this huge tax grab in the name of self-sufficiency which never occurred.

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald J. Johnston (President of the Treasury Board):
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity of participating in the debate on the budget to bring to the attention of hon. members the viewpoint as it were of the Treasury Board and the President of the Treasury Board, and to focus on some aspects of the budget which are particularly important from
The Budget-Mr. Johnston
the Treasury Board perspective and from the over-all management aspect of the finances of the federal government.
Hon. members will recall that in 1976 the Liberal government of the day established the Royal Commission on Financial Management and Accountability, headed by Allan Lambert who, at the time, was chairman of the Toronto Dominion Bank. The Lambert commission, as it is commonly known, had very broad terms of reference, and its objective was to improve the over-all management and accountability of the federal government. It was asked to examine and recommend a mutually compatible management system appropriate to government in the interrelated areas of financial management, control and accountability, including accountability of deputy ministers and heads of Crown agencies.

The commission's mandate was also to examine interdepartmental structures, the organization of central agencies serving departments and Crown corporations and related procedures, as well as the financial management policy, rules, guidelines and procedures applied by central agencies to determine whether accountability, both within government and to Parliament, is ensured.

As we all know, the Lambert commission produced its final report, containing some 165 recommendations, in March,
1979.	The report was well received by all parties in this House. It is a credit to the commissioners and their staff that this was the case.
In April, 1980, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) asked me to co-ordinate the government's response to the Lambert report. I am pleased to report to hon. members that we have made considerable progress in this regard and are currently working on a target date of the end of the year in terms of a comprehensive response to the Lambert recommendations. I would like to point out that 1 have been very ably assisted in this work by Mr. W. A. B. Anderson, who was formerly a senior deputy minister of the province of Ontario, and for that I would like to give credit to the hon. member for Wellington-Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Beatty) who, while minister of state for the Treasury Board, had the foresight to appoint Mr. Anderson to this most important post.
I said that we have made considerable progress in reviewing and implementing the recommendations of the Lambert report and, indeed, we have. Very tangible evidence of this was contained in the budget presented by my colleague, the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen), last Tuesday, October 28,
1980.	The expenditure plan contained in the budget is very much consistent with the recommendations of the Lambert commission. For the first time we have been able to set out the agreed planning levels for each major category of expenditure or envelope with a multi-year horizon.
Under the new policy and expenditure management system the policy committees of cabinet will plan their activities over an extended period of years and, within the framework of that plan, will make policy and related financial decisions together.

November 3, 1980
The Budget-Mr. Johnston
Policy committees will have to fund new, high priority initiatives from their envelopes, so they will be demanding and will be critical in their evaluation of existing programs within the federal government. In turn, I believe, this will create an increased onus on managers to develop full information and cost implications of their policy proposals and to manage efficiently and effectively within their established limits.
Unlike my predecessor, the hon. member for York-Peel (Mr. Stevens), who kept trying to assume the responsibilities, in my judgment, of the Minister of Finance, I readily acknowledge the lead role of the Minister of Finance in developing the fiscal plan. I recognize, too, the primary and critical role that the Treasury Board of Canada has in supporting the policy and expenditure management system which has come of age with this budget. Let me highlight briefly for you a number of recent initiatives taken by the government which are complementary and, indeed, essential to the success of this new top-down, multi-year system.
The first area is what I would call the process of departmental improvement. In 1978 the government appointed a Comptroller General of Canada. The first Comptroller General, Mr. Harry Rogers, very quickly took some significant steps to define problems and plan improvements in the management processes of the many departments of the federal government. In particular, I refer to the IMPAC surveys with which many hon. members are familiar, and the departmental action plans which have emerged from it. The IMPAC action plan has become the prime executive tool for strengthening management practices in many departments.

Most of us are aware of the fact that the IMPAC study was initially concerned with the management pratices of 29 major federal departments. This initial phase lead to a memorandum of agreement between deputy ministers and the Comptroller General on the improvements to be made. The study has now reached the phase at which action plans are being developed and the focus of attention is on the identification of means necessary to bring about the required changes.
The action plans the departments have developed within the study cover several factors such as the establishment of a strict planning process, the development and integration of operational and financial information systems, the monitoring of activities according to plans, the establishment of program evaluation functions and the broadening of internal auditing activities. All these sectors to be improved upon are compatible with the requests made to the departments in the context of the reforms I have just mentioned.

The second element would be regarded as improved reporting to Parliament, which is particularly significant for the members of this chamber.
The government has recognized the importance of providing Parliament and the public with high quality information to
assess the major decisions which will emerge from the new policy and expenditure management program. The proposed legislation on access to information, and the project to revise the estimates and the public accounts, are evidence of the effort this government is making to improve the information available to Parliament and to the public.
[ Translation]
It is not easy, Mr. Speaker, to decide the way in which information is to be submitted. A quick glance at the blue book will show the complexity of the government's programs and activities. At the moment, the office of the Comptroller General is examining a general model for submitting estimates, which is being tried by five departments. The first results of this experiment should be known in the near future. [English]
Another aspect of this approach is program evaluation. As I mentioned earlier, and as the Minister of Finance emphasized in his budget speech, the new policy and expenditure management system creates an incentive to find ways of saving money in existing programs in order to finance new high priority activities. Basically, in program evaluation, the government must answer fundamental questions about a program:
[ Translation]
Has the program met its objectives? Did it have unforeseen, positive or negative, effects? Could those objectives be reached with the same resources but with different means? Should the program be pursued in its present form?

I am pleased to report that under the guidance of the office of the Comptroller General, departments are well on the way to setting up organizations for the conduct of program evaluation.
Another aspect which must not be forgotten is personnel management for the eighties. I am sure that hon. members will agree that the new policy and expenditure management system, or any system for that matter, will only be as good as the people who run it. At the very foundation of the system is good personnel management-the hiring, training, and development of good people. In this regard I have said publicly on several occasions, and believe strongly, that we are building on strengths within our public service. I have been much impressed by the high degree of competence, willingness, and dedication that I have found in the public service. With this as a strong starting base, I have recently taken several steps in Treasury Board toward better personnel management in the federal government.

The federal government is now creating a separate category for senior managers in the federal public service. This innovation has as its main component an integrated evaluation system which provides for rewards or penalties according to the accountability for effective realization of government program objectives.
November 3, 1980



At the same time we are implementing a staff training and development policy which strengthens the assessment of training needs, improves the content and conduct of training courses within the public service, and ensures post-training evaluation and feedback.
Just last week, I announced a landmark new part-time employment policy designed to foster the use of employees on a part-time basis and draw into the public service much of this unused talent, particularly working mothers. This program will, 1 believe, be of particular benefit to those who wish to combine a meaningful professional career with important family responsibilities.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
In his budget address the Minister of Finance reaffirmed, as I do, the commitment of this government to keep the general operating expenses of the federal government and person years under close control. This will require the achievement of further increases in productivity. Hon. members will know that it was for this reason that we have resisted demands in some cases for a shorter work week in the public service. Increased productivity is essential for a strong economic recovery and the federal government must take the lead in this regard.
As I just said, this government will, as a priority, continue to keep its general operating expenses under close control. But I would not want to leave the impression with hon. members or with the public that the direct operating expenses of the government, per se, will offer a dramatic source of savings in the coming years. I emphasize the term "dramatic". Over the past five years, as the House is aware, the federal government has done commendably well in controlling its operating expenses, to the extent that there is relatively very little room left for improvement in this component of federal expenditures. Consider the following breakdown of our expenditures: [Translation]
More than half of the expenditures in the main estimates, or about $30 million for the 1980-81 fiscal year, is made up of transfers to other government levels or individuals or of grants. [English]
The two major components of federal transfers, as you well know, Mr. Speaker, consist of transfers to other governments, being equalization payments under federal-provincial fiscal arrangements, and established programs financing. The latter, often known as EPF, covers hospital insurance, medical care, and post-secondary education. These three major programs are administered by the provinces but are financed in part by the federal government.
The largest single element of federal subsidies is payments under the oil import compensation program, first introduced in 1973-74, to provide compensation to importers of crude oil in order to ensure a uniform domestic price of oil that is below the international price. Any unexpected jump in international prices or an unforeseen fall in the exchange rate, entails an
The Budget-Mr. Johnston
increase in the level of expenditures under the OICP program. Roughly, a $1 per barrel rise in international prices, or a three-cent decline in the Canadian dollar, if sustained under that existing regime, would raise outlays by some $200 million. Understandably, my colleague, the Minister of Finance, found it necessary to meet this issue head on in his budget. The major component of federal transfers to persons is payment of benefits to the aged under the old age security, guaranteed income supplement, and spouse's allowances programs. Family allowance payments are another major element of federal transfers to individuals.
Second, Mr. Speaker, the interests on the public debt are expected to reach $10.3 billion in 1980-81, which represent 17.7 per cent of total budgetary expenditures.
Third, the payments to public corporations will reach $2.4 billion in 1980-81, or 4.1 per cent of total budgetary expenditures.
Fourth, the government operating and capital expenditures will amount to $15.5 billion in 1980-81, which represents 26.8 per cent of the public expenditures. This is a reduction of 1.4 per cent compared with the percentage for goods and services last year.
All in all, more than 83 per cent of the increase in budgetary expenditures for the present fiscal year will be used for transfer payments to other governments, individuals and Canadian companies, or for public debt charges. Government operating costs, with the exception of national defence, represent only 7 per cent of the total increase in budgetary expenditures for the fiscal year 1980-81.

It seems clear from what I have said that if further significant reductions in federal expenditures are required, they will not be in the area of direct government operations. That does not mean we will not continue to seek out more efficient means of delivering services to the public, but major dramatic savings will not be effected in those areas.
In conclusion, as President of the Treasury Board and member of Parliament for St. Henri-Westmount, I would like to commend the Minister of Finance for the very fine budget delivered last week. All Canadians will welcome the frank and open way in which he has presented his expenditure plan and his medium term economic assumptions.
Also, I am sure that all Canadians will welcome the continuing commitment of this government to expenditure restraint and to further increases in productivity.
While much of the attention during this debate will focus on the issue of energy and other areas of the budget, I hope this milestone will not escape the attention of members, the publication of a multiyear fiscal plan envelope by envelope, which

November 3, 1980
The Budget-Mr. Benjamin
indeed is a landmark in the history of financial management in Canada.
