subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The refundable energy tax credit was a very important part of the Crosbie budget. What that would have meant to Canadians earning under $21,380 is that an average family with two children would have had a tax rebate cash credit of $220. The two cents a gallon more in the cost of gasoline under the past government's program would have worked out to about 600 gallons a year at 12,000 miles per year, assuming your automobile gets 20 miles to the gallon, which works out to about $12 a year, give or take a few miles. The fact of the matter is that an average family of four would have been the recipients of about $220 in a cash credit under the old program. This means that under the Crosbie budget, the average Canadian family, at the end of 1983, would have been $208 better off per year than under the present minister's budget.
What else do we have in that package? We also have those nefarious little goodies which were referred to as the Canadian ownership charge. We have not been told much about the Canadian ownership charge, except that it is one to which we will all contribute so that we all end up owning some grandiose multinational oil company, getting into the oil business in a big way and becoming real social democrats. There are one or two other programs which are not defined as well. It is hard to say just exactly what it will mean. Before it is all over, I suspect that the 18-cent excise tax which defeated the Conservative government last February 18 will look like a Sunday school picnic in comparison to what we will have to pay under the present government.
Does anyone in the House of Commons recall the present government telling the people during the last campaign that it would increase the taxes on heating oil? I did not hear them, and no one I talked to on the street heard them either. But it is a fact of life. The fact is there has been an annual tax on heating oil which by the end of 1983 will amount to 36 cents per gallon more than would have been imposed under the Crosbie budget. It will mean an additional increase of approximately $286 per annum for the average family. Do hon. members opposite realize that? I bet it did not appear anywhere in their campaign material. Certainly it did not appear in any newspaper advertisement which I read. No, they did not
4386

November 3, 1980
The Budget-Mr. Corbett
mention that type of thing, but we are used to that approach by the government.
What has happened to the program for the conversion of oil to gas? This is probably one of the more positive points of the budget, one I would like to take a few minutes to address. It is outlined in the book entitled: "The National Energy Program". Page 56 reads in part as follows:
For conversions from oil to gas, electricity, renewable, and other energy sources, a grant of 50 per cent of the conversion cost, up to a maximum of $800.
It goes on to say:
However, the program will take account of special situations in individual provinces. For example, the dependence of the Atlantic provinces on oil for electrical generation, although declining, precludes financial assistance for conversion to electricity at this time.
The last sentence of the third paragraph on page 57 tell us:
No one should delay action to convert away from oil.
I can only presume from this that even maritimers in this particular instance are not being regarded by the government as second-class citizens. I am very thankful for that. The sentence before that one reads as follows:
When the program is operational, compensation will be paid.
I think that is a positive step. I look forward to many maritimers, many New Brunswickers, taking advantage of the program.
Under the section dealing with the Atlantic provinces, we read on page 86:
Assistance will be provided to consumers, as in other provinces, to switch from oil to other fuels. Assistance for conversions to electric heating will not be immediately available in the Atlantic region, however.
In the province of New Brunswick more than half of its generated power comes from sources other than oil. Yet, according to this, for some reason or another New Brunswickers will be denied this program to convert to electricity from oil, despite the fact that less than half the electricity produced in the province of New Brunswick comes from oil. I should like the minister to take notice of this.
I understand that over the weekend there was a Liberal rally in my constituency of Fundy-Royal, at which time the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Cosgrove) attended as the guest speaker. A resolution was passed at that particular rally asking that the Minister of Public Works contact the Minister of Finance and implore him to allow the Atlantic region access to the same program as the rest of Canada. Obviously the implications were that they had not taken the time or bothered to read the national energy program to determine that Atlantic Canadians are indeed entitled to compensation for switching to other forms of energy with the exception of electricity. Perhaps the good minister would like to take their suggestion under advisement. I hope he will allow Atlantic Canadians the same opportunities in this nation as other Canadians. But I doubt that this will actually be a fact of life.
The minister represents a part of the country which is very rich in coal. Apparently he has lots of money to deal out and has become very generous with the part of the country he represents, Cape Breton. I think that is laudable, it is very
noble of the minister. It has been a hard pressed area in the past, and I am thankful and pleased for the people of Cape Breton that the minister has taken cognizance of the fact their coal reserves should be developed. But there are other regions in the maritime provinces which have coal as well.
In my constituency the regions of Minto and Chipman have coal reserves. Last May 2 I asked the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) if it was his intention or the government's intention to aid in the extraction, production and/or marketing of coal from the Minto and Chipman areas. The answer was no, that the department had no plans to aid in the extraction, production and/or marketing of coal from those areas of New Brunswick at that time. I can assure the minister that the miners and their families in the Minto and Chipman areas of New Brunswick like to eat just as well as the miners of Cape Breton. I think they should be given the same opportunities and favouritism as the minister has shown to the people residing in his constituency.
There are energy resources in New Brunswick besides coal. In Albert county there is oil shale which has been producing oil since 1922. Also there are gas reserves in that county which have produced natural gas for use in the Hillsborough area for a good number of years. Where is this mentioned in the budget or in the national energy program developed by the Minister of Finance for the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources? It is conveniently forgotten, like the commitment to DREE. The government was committed to eliminating regional disparities, but it did not take into consideration doing anything additional for the Department of Regional Economic Expansion. He talked about the manufacturers' investment tax credit. This was done in consultation with his good friend and old crony, the minister. This was for specifically designated areas. Indeed, it will be interesting to see where those specifically designated areas are.
There was no mention of the national parks in this country. We have a beautiful park in Fundy-Royal, which is suffering from a lack of attendance and has been over the last few years.
1 would have liked to have seen some attention brought to the plight of parks such as Fundy in order to increase attendance. But, no, not a word about it. Today it is appropriate to bring up the subject of national parks because we have park superintendents from all across this land visiting us here in the nation's capital. I would have liked to have seen some thought addressed to the plight of parks such as Fundy, but there was nothing.
What about the farmers of this country? There was hardly a mention made of farmers. The farmers are one of the most maligned groups of individuals in the nation. Yet there was hardly a word. The same thing can be said of fishermen.
And what about all of the poor people of this country? We do have them, in case the minister is not aware. There are poor people in this country who find it difficult to make ends meet and to get a meal. Where are the breaks for the little guys? Again, I should be asking the NDP who made all the rest of this possible for the people of Canada.
November 3, 1980

Where are the programs such as the mortgage interest and property tax credit plan which was included in the Crosbie budget? Where is the energy tax credit plan that would have helped the little guy absorb his new taxes? No, they are not there, Mr. Speaker. What about the heating fuel increases? These are the types of things we should be considering. We have only the assurance of higher inflation, higher taxes and more government spending. It is a one-man medicine show and a poor one at that. It is a spoof on professional quackery and this government, this minister, should not be allowed to get away with it.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it gives me a great deal of pleasure to participate in this debate, which is on the first budget of the 1980s. This budget is the first of its kind in that it combines two priorities which are of increasing importance to this country. They are finances and energy. The link between has become such that it is impossible nowadays to separate them. Energy and finances will dominate the 1980s and our ability to effectively deal with them will have a direct bearing on whether or not we survive this century as a united federation.
This budget is the logical conclusion of our election campaign of last winter. Unlike some of the opposition members, who believe in instant cures to complex problems, we did not go charging off around the country making empty promises to the people of Canada which we could not keep. Rather, we anticipated the future. We realized that the people of Canada sought and demanded a government that could put the country of Canada back on its feet. We are a government which realized that election promises were just like any other promises made in good faith-they are made to be kept.
Just what did we promise the people of Canada? We promised them three things. First, we promised energy security at a fair price to all Canadians. Second, we promised to keep government expenditures within the rate of growth of the economy. Finally, we promised an orderly reduction of the deficit. Well, Mr. Speaker, we delivered on each and every one of those promises. This budget is a Liberal budget in every sense of the word. It is fair to all Canadians. It sets forth an energy program that will help Canadians reach energy selfsufficiency at a fair, made-in-Canada price. It holds the line on government expenditures while providing aid in those areas that need it most. In short, it lends direction to Canada at a time when it is crucial that this country should realize where it is going and the best way to get there. This budget calls to mind something which was said over a hundred years ago by Thomas D'Arcy McGee. He said:
The government must lead as well as save; it must march as well as fortify; it must originate plans for the future, as well as correct the errors of the past.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that that quotation describes as well as any what this budget does for Canada.
It is important to realize that it is virtually impossible to separate energy policies from fiscal policies when constructing a budget. Perhaps this is the case in Canada more than in any other western country. Economics and energy are the meat and potatoes issues of the 1980s. By dealing with both at the
The Budget-Mr. Bloomfield
same time the government is prescribing a complete comprehensive remedy for the country's current malaise. During the previous election we campaigned on these fiscal reforms and we were elected to this House as a majority. To fail to present this type of budget would be to shirk our responsibilities to ourselves and, most important, to the people of Canada.
As I said earlier, the government's expenditures program will be aimed at helping those who need help most. They are the senior citizens of Canada. To this end we have already raised the guaranteed income supplement by some $35 per household. That is what we promised in the last campaign. That is what we delivered in the first session of this Parliament.
Another group which desperately needs help is the small businessman. In the past we have been dedicated to helping the small businessman in various ways, one example of this being the ceiling raised on the small loans legislation from $75,000 to $100,000. In this budget the small business development bonds program has been extended. This will help reduce the costs of small business corporations. In all sectors of the industry I cannot think of any that is more important, more fundamental or more vital to Canada than the small business sector. It is the backbone of our economy, the birthplace of innovation and the focal point of industrial ingenuity. We, as Liberals, are aware of the important function the small business entrepreneur plays in Canadian society. We are committed to providing a healthy environment in which small business can grow and flourish.
In the field of economic development we have allocated some $350 million, a 22 per cent increase, to aid research and development and to supplement industrial restructuring. Also, a program designed to increase Canada's pool of domestic skilled tradesmen will be implemented. I might add that these training programs could have been avoided had the provinces recognized Canada's needs for a skilled labour force instead of encouraging all of their young people to attend university.
With respect to research and development I am happy we are allocating some funds to deal specifically with that issue. It is very interesting to note that Canada leads her economic summit partners in terms of government sponsored R and D expenditures as a percentage of gross national product. However, she lags behind in industry-sponsored research and development. In my view, this should be changed. Canada needs more research and development, whether it be government or privately sponsored. This helps Canada maintain her international competitive edge in terms of manufacturing. However, we must not allow ourselves to become complacent about our commitment to research and development. Germany and Japan have become considerably more successful in their conquest of world markets. Our high technology, communications and nuclear industries must continue to strive for excellence if we are to maintain our already prestigious international reputation. I look forward to the increased co-operation between government and industry to achieve this goal in the future.

November 3, 1980
The Budget-Mr. Bloomfield
We, in Canada, cannot forget the fact that we are, in many ways, one of the most fortunate peoples on the globe. We are not starving, as they are in southeast Asia. We are not living in the shadow of communism, as are the peoples of Afghanistan and Sweden. Nor are we subjected to the tyranny of a dictatorial regime, as are people in other parts of the world. It is important that we do not forget our international duties in terms of aid to countries which are less fortunate than we. Accordingly, this government is committed to increase our foreign aid to .5 per cent of our GNP by the end of fiscal 1984.
In the field of national defence, we will be increasing our expenditures by 3 per cent in real terms and this will apply directly to our NATO commitments. I heartily embrace this policy. I, for one, do not believe in starting a war with anyone. Neither am I of the opinion that we in the free world should let our defences crumble and decay at a time when Soviet aggression has never been so flagrant. Our western defence capabilities must not become suspect.
Through these programs, Mr. Speaker, we have shown Canada a path to economic recovery; a path that balances fiscal restraint with industrial incentives which will, if combined with our energy program, guarantee a stronger Canada in the future.
The new energy policy will, when fully implemented, ensure that, indeed, Canada will no longer have to depend on a foreign cartel for our oil. Allow me to quote from the national energy program highlights:
Three basic objectives guide our decisions:
(1)	Security of supply and ultimate energy independence;
(2)	Opportunity for Canadians to participate in energy industries, especially
oil and gas;
(3)	Fairness in pricing and the sharing of revenues among governments and
industry.
This is just what we told the Canadian people we would do. Through such existing government agencies as PetroCan, and other new ones, we will be able to provide Canada and Canadians with both economic stimulus and petroleum products that have a made-in-Canada price. This is a bold, courageous new program and one that most suits Canadian requirements. It is the type of program that promises to leave Canada in a good position to become self-sufficient in oil in the foreseeable future.
This debate is designed to present, in a logical manner, the goals of our national energy program. In doing so, it is hoped we will alleviate the reluctance of the western provinces to go along with our proposals. Basically, we believe that Canadians should be treated fairly and equally across the land and that it is the federal government's responsibility to make sure that this happens. Until 1973 there was no problem in maintaining this equality and fairness. When there was a world surplus of oil between 1957 and 1970, the federal government pursued policies that required industry to increase their use of domestic, higher cost crude oil even though cheaper imported oil was readily available. For this and other reasons, the pipeline from the west to Ontario was built.
In 1973 when the price of imported oil skyrocketed, the federal government concluded a new oil pricing agreement witht he producing provinces and undertook to compensate non-producing provinces for more expensive imported oil. During this time, the producing provinces amassed huge revenues as the Canadian government went deeper and deeper into debt through equalization payments. At the same time the foreign multinationals also increased their revenues. The old formula of revenue sharing, which saw the provinces and oil companies each take 45 per cent of the revenues, left the federal government with a meager 10 per cent to support the non-producing provinces.
At present the system is nearing complete breakdown. Without wanting to intrude on provincial revenues, the federal government must find new sources of revenues if the equalization system is to continue. This brings us to the present. The multinationals control a disproportionate amount of the revenues. Through the sale of Canadian petroleum products and through various tax shelters, they are shipping $4 of every $5 out of the country at Canada's expense. The profits that they are reaping are truly incredible. For example, the six largest oil companies in Canada, all foreign controlled, represent 71.7 per cent of the Canadian petroleum industry. Internal cash flow for these companies rose 43.6 per cent in 1979. After tax profits were up 53.8 per cent from the previous year.
Mr. Speaker, I do not mind a pig, but I hate a hog. We must stop this flow of capital out of the country and start back on the road to recovery. Through PetroCan and other government agencies we can commence an orderly Canadianization program for the petroleum industry. Such a program is not unknown in the world today. In Norway, Statoil controls from 50 per cent to 70 per cent of that country's petroleum industry and in Australia at least 25 per cent of the industry is domestically owned. The list continues.
It is important to keep in mind the fact that by Canadianiz-ing the industry, the provinces have little to lose. We propose a new split of 43 per cent to the producing provinces, 33 per cent to industry, and 24 per cent to the federal government. On top of this the producing provinces will receive many economic benefits to help diversify their economies and prepare for the future when oil and natural gas reserves are depleted.
The western development fund is a program aimed at achieving this goal. Four billion dollars, of which $2 billion will be allocated between now and 1983, will be set aside to fund projects selected jointly by the federal government and the governments of the producing provinces. Another commitment made by the federal government is the creation of a natural gas bank. This will provide smaller, Canadian-owned companies, with an early market for their natural gas. As well, it will help generate their cash flow in order that they may continue exploration and development. Coupled with this is the promotion of a conversion program to help Canada move off oil to natural gas.
In order to provide the producing provinces with new markets for their natural gas while stimulating Canada's economy at the same time, a network of pipeline construction will be
November 3, 1980

initiated by the federal government. Most notable of these is the Q & M pipeline which will ultimately bring western natural gas to the maritime provinces. 1 would suggest that if eastern reserves are proven, as they are, this pipeline be designed to bring eastern oil westward.
In putting together this comprehensive energy package, it becomes glaringly evident that the producing provinces, indeed all of Canada, will benefit considerably. The producing provinces stand to gain $38 billion, with Alberta receiving $31 billion. The petroleum industry will collect $30 billion and the federal government will collect $24 billion. Canadians will no longer be subjected to OPEC price shocks and we will be able to plot a course towards oil independence.
Through the expansion of PetroCan we will progress from a country dominated by foreign multinationals to a nation that is both self-reliant in energy and self-assured in the future. The Canadian energy industry will be more responsive to Canadian realities and requirements. The decision to implement this bold, new energy fiscal policy is the culmination of many months of careful planning and analysis. If successful, it will provide Canadians with substantially less-than-world energy prices and lend a tremendous edge to our other industries. Once implemented, it will then be up to Canadians to grasp the ball and run with it; without the co-operation from every citizen in the land, Canada runs the risk of squandering this unique opportunity to fashion her own destiny. This would be most unfortunate.
We are entering a new era, a time when opportunities such as this rarely present themselves. I urge all Canadians whether they be from the west, the east or the centre of Canada, to put down their regional barriers and come together under this plan for the future. Together we are stronger; united we cannot be subjugated by external economic forces. Let us embrace each other as brothers in this blessed country called Canada and become that for which our forefathers toiled so hard; one nation, rich in our diversity, but ever cognizant of the mutual goals that bind us.

subtopic: PENSIONS REVIEW BOARD-INQUIRY RESPECTING INCREASE IN STAFF
PENSIONS REVIEW BOARD-INQUIRY RESPECTING INCREASE IN STAFF
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on October 17 of this year I requested that the acting Minister of Veterans Affairs bring the Pensions Review Board up to strength. I am happy to say that the minister took immediate action after I raised the matter in the House. I hope he will
Adjournment Debate
take such swift action in regard to the Bureau of Pensions Advocates which is also understaffed.
In a letter to the chief executive officer of The War Amputations of Canada regarding the Pensions Review Board the minister stated, in part, as follows:
the board is now at full strength. With extensive training for the next two months, Mr. Jutras expects to have all members fully operative. By late fall the board should be in a position to do better than meet the current demand.
I should like to quote from the Veterans Affairs Annual Report 1978-79. Under the heading "Years Activities" there appears the following:
During the fiscal year the board received 1,374 appeal applications (including 24 applications to vary previous decisions), compared with 1,286 the previous year.
It heard a total of 1,076 cases, including two interpretation hearings. The total for the previous year was 874. It rendered 1,071 decisions (in 1978, 878). Approximately 86 per cent of its decisions confirmed the decisions of the commission, about the same percentage as in the previous year. The decisions dealt with a total of 2,115 disabilities-
This means, Mr. Speaker, that the board is approximately 27 per cent behind in its work of reviewing applications. That being the case, the two additional board members will certainly help the situation. As it takes about two years to train a board member, I should like to suggest to the minister that the Pension Act be amended to permit the appointment of two additional temporary board members for a period of years until the time taken to process appeals is back to normal. These two members would be in addition to the seven provided for in the act.
The Canadian Legion, army, navy and air force veterans, and The War Amputations of Canada are deeply concerned about the delays in processing claims. In a recent letter to the late minister of veterans affairs, The War Amputations of Canada pointed out that a large number of war amputees died before their pension appeals could be reviewed. Over the past eight years 370 applicants died before their applications could be processed.
There were also delays in Ontario in the processing of claims for increased pension benefits. District DVA offices throughout Ontario are encountering problems in securing departmental files from the regional office in Toronto. The Royal Canadian Legion has discussed this matter with the deputy minister. For months, assurances have been given that everyone is trying to correct the staffing problem which is seemingly the root of the situation at the regional office in Toronto. I hope the minister will take steps to see that appropriate action is taken. I am presently working on a case where the veteran has been waiting seven months for a review of his claim.
I hope the minister has good news for us tonight regarding these very lengthy delays in the processing of veterans claims, Mr. Speaker.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. Gilles Lamontagne (Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Minister of National Defence
subtopic: PENSIONS REVIEW BOARD-INQUIRY RESPECTING INCREASE IN STAFF
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 thank the member from Winnipeg-Assiniboine (Mr. McKenzie) for the opportunity to clarify the staff situation at the Pensions Review Board.

November 3, 1980
Adjournment Debate
As hon. members may know, the board was established under the 1971 amendments to the Pension Act. It is exclusively an independent appeal tribunal reporting directly to Parliament through the Minister of Veterans Affairs. The Pensions Review Board has authority to determine any question of law or fact as to whether a person is entitled to an award under the act, and the amount of any such award, and the decision of the board is final and binding for all purposes of the act.
In a letter dated October 17, 1980, I informed the chief executive officer of The War Amputations of Canada that the Pensions Review Board is now at full strength. With extensive training for the next few months, the chairman of the Pensions Review Board expects to have all members fully operative. By late fall the board should be in a position to meet the current demand of cases. Hon. members may recall that in 1977 the Pension Act was amended to provide an additional two members to the board. The board presently hears five to seven cases per day and this number is expected to rise slightly when all members are fully trained and operative. I can assure all members that the board will work as quickly as possible, keeping in mind the necessity to ensure each veteran appealing a claim the best service possible.
The Bureau of Pensions Advocates provides a free legal aid service to persons seeking to establish claims under the Pension Act and the Civilian War Pension and Allowances Acts. Presently the bureau is operating at full strength with the possibility of one vacancy occurring in one of the bureau's field offices early next year. With the known and anticipated claims for pensions from veterans and widows, the chief pensions advocate is confident that the work load will be handled with the same degree of care as the bureau has consistently demonstrated over the years. If delays are still experienced in spite of what 1 just mentioned, we will take steps to correct the situation as soon as we can.

Mr. Speaker, on June 27, 1980, I asked the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) to conduct an inquiry into regional air policy. My reason for requesting a review by the minister was that the cabinet had just that day announced a decision whereby it had overruled a decision of the Canadian Transport Commission in respect of the right of CP Air to fly between Halifax and Toronto. The result of the cabinet decision permitted Eastern Provincial Airways to fly direct on the Halifax-Toronto route.
While I agree with the substance of that decision, I was concerned, as were others, that the whole difficulty arose from confusion about regional air policy. It is very important that such an inquiry be made and that the minister review all aspects of the regional air policy.
The minister indicated in the House on June 27, 1980, that he did not propose to make a specific and formal investigation.
He subsequently indicated he was asking government departments involved, the air carriers and others involved in the air industry, to express their views on regional air policy. I would like to take a few moments to outline some of the concerns that must be related to a new regional air transport policy.
The importance of the regional air transport industry to Nova Scotia and Atlantic Canada should not be underestimated. Let us start with the Halifax international airport which today has 75 daily commercial flights. It handles on an annual basis about 1.5 million passengers. It is equal in that respect to Mirabel, but I hope it is not the same in other respects. There are 1,700 employees who work at the Halifax international airport and the work force is building on a daily basis as new inquiries come in.
A recent report by the task force on airport management recommended more local autonomy for airports. This is a big factor in the future expansion of our airport business across Canada, that there be more local autonomy-not that the federal Department of Transport be allowed to escape its responsibilities in the air transport field. In Halifax we have a great port which is promoted by locals. It involves trade sojourns across the world to attract business. We could use this kind of activity in relation to our airport.
I want to take a moment to commend Eastern Provincial Airways on the work they are doing and the contribution they are making to the local economy, employing over 900 employees in Atlantic Canada and spending $10 million in the Halifax area alone. One of their ambitions is to be involved in the takeover of Nordair which is now controlled by Air Canada and which has a $30 million price tag on it. Others in the bidding include Quebec and Ontario interests.
The Minister of Transport said there must be a balance of interest. I hope he will see his way clear in the future to give complete consideration to the bid made by Eastern Provincial Airways because this could be a big contribution to the air transport business in Atlantic Canada and put it on a firm base.
CP Air has now decided to take up the decision of the Canadian Transport Commission and exercise its right to land in Halifax. We welcome CP Air to the east coast. We hope it will make a real contribution. They should be reminded that what we require is employment and local-based activity, not just simply flights from Toronto and Montreal with landings in Halifax. 1 know they will take this into consideration. I hope they will be able to expand into the international markets. In that connection also we welcome British Airways to Halifax and Halifax International Airport. It was announced in September, 1980, that British Airways had been granted landing rights in Halifax and we hope that this will expand international trade.
Of great importance to our air transport economy in Atlantic Canada is Air Canada. We are proud of the contribution made by Air Canada and its local employees in Halifax West. We are proud that the dedicated staff at the airport provide
November 3, 1980

such good service. We welcome the recent addition to the airport facility and staff of over 180 flight attendants. We hope that within the near future Air Canada will see fit to locate pilots and other flight crew members in the Halifax area.
However, something is happening nationally to Air Canada which is of great concern to all of us. International, Air Canada is slipping in rank. It is ranked fourteenth by North American passengers. Many complain that Air Canada s service is deteriorating. Evidence before the Dubin inquiry indicated that air safety is sometimes compromised and many of us are concerned as to how Air Canada is being operated. There are those who even suggest that language qualifications take precedence over skills in some areas. I fear that Air Canada's request for greater revenue and a reduction of expenses is at the root of these complaints. I warn Air Canada that if it compromises passenger safety by cost-cutting measures, Canadians will rise up and complain as a group, and action will have to be taken.
We want Air Canada to play a role in the regional air transport service. We want Air Canada to be successful as a national and an international carrier. However, it will have to clean up its act, give better service and contribute more in the future.

speakeroldname: Mr. Robert Bockstael (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member's question in the House on June 27 appeared to indicate that he was not dissatisfied with the minister's announcement that EPA would be granted the Halifax-Toronto route. He confirmed that this evening.
In announcing the decision, the minister stressed the need to improve EPA's economic potential by allowing it to broaden its route structure. He also noted that CP Air would have access to Halifax from any point on its transcontinental licence, except Toronto. Those features would benefit Atlantic Canada by providing better access and promoting tourist traffic in the region.
As the hon. member knows the decision was well received in the east. Furthermore, as he indicated this evening, after an initial hesitation, CP Air has decided to take advantage of the opportunity and recently announced a Montreal-Halifax service to begin in March 1981.
In his question, the hon. member mentioned the current review of regional air carrier policy. The review was undertaken as a result of fundamental changes in the structure of the domestic air carrier industry, for instance, the merger of PWA and Transair, the extension of Nordair services to Winnipeg and the potential effects of the resale of Nordair to the private sector, just to mention a few. Such a review can be a lengthy process. The decision on the Halifax-Toronto route obviously could not be put off indefinitely. It is the minister's hope that the review can be completed in the coming months so that uncertainties of this kind can be minimized in the future.
I will relay to the minister the concerns which the hon. member for Halifax West (Mr. Crosby) has expressed this
Adjournment Debate
evening. I can assure him that it is the policy of the Ministry of Transport and of Air Canada never to reduce concern for the safety of passengers for economic reasons.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to follow up a question I asked in this House on April 28 last of the Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan) with respect to the question of mail opening by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. In doing so I referred to yet an earlier question, at which time the Solicitor General indicated that there would be a report forthcoming with respect to certain evidence as to the advisability of permitting the RCMP to engage in the opening of the mail of Canadians.
I might say that, unfortunately, I believe, we witnessed undue haste on the part of the Solicitor General in stating that in his view the RCMP did need this particular power. It was within a few days of being sworn in as Solicitor General that the present Solicitor General stated he was convinced that the mail of Canadians should be subject to opening by the RCMP, a practice which, as we have seen through evidence at the McDonald commission, has been taking place on an illegal scale for some considerable length of time. The Solicitor General said he believed that on the basis of his conversations, limited as they were, with the commissioner of the RCMP and others this power was warranted.
At that time, I and others asked what evidence there was to warrant the granting of permission for this invasion of the fundamental privacy of Canadians? We were told at that point that a report would be forthcoming. We were told that the RCMP had been requested to provide a full and comprehensive report to the Solicitor General outlining the grounds for their request that the RCMP have the right to open the first-class private mail of Canadians. I should also point out that when the representatives of the RCMP were asked before the McDonald commission why they felt it was necessary to break the law of the land and intercept the first-class mail of Canadians, and when they were asked to produce evidence as to why they broke the law in that respect, members of the security service came up with nothing.
They came up with an excuse which, as it later turned out, was totally spurious. They were able to give but a single example of the use of mail opening to detect and prevent a possible crime. That example was the detection of possible terrorist activity on the part of a certain "Japanese Red Army" member in Canada. It was with great pride that this example was flourished before the McDonald commission by an RCMP member. There was rather subdued silence, though, when it was learned that mail opening had had nothing whatsoever to do with the apprehending of that particular potential criminal and that it was because of wire tap evidence that that possible crime was uncovered. So before the McDonald Commission not a scintilla of evidence was produced to justify the request of the RCMP for legal mail opening powers

November 3, 1980
Adjournment Debate
or to justify actions they have been pursuing for some considerable time in this country on a illegal basis.
We suggested to the Solicitor General that since no evidence was presented before the McDonald commission, he must surely have some grounds to warrant his enthusiasm for this sweeping power to be granted to the RCMP. The Solicitor General said he expected a report to reach him soon. We finally asked him where that report was. Lo and behold, a report had been submitted to the Solicitor General, but he did not like what he saw. In fact, what he saw was so inconsequential and so weak that he had to send it back to the RCMP saying, "This is not good enough; I cannot in all conscience bring this to the Parliament of Canada as a justification for asking for mail opening powers". He sent it back to the RCMP and assured Parliament that there would be another report forthcoming in the very near future. That was in April of this year. Since that time what have we heard to justify the zealous request for mail opening powers by the RCMP? Silence. Where is this much-heralded report of the RCMP which would justify the powers for which the Solicitor General has asked? It is nowhere.
We were told that this fundamental invasion of the privacy of Canadians would have to await a report. We were also told-and this is very important-that no legislative action would be taken on mail opening until such time as the McDonald commission has reported on this and certain other investigative techniques.
One would have hoped that the government would have stuck to that commitment. But no. In fact, before any report from the RCMP or from the McDonald commission, we see an attempt to legitimize through the back door mail opening in certain circumstances. I refer to an amendment to the Post Office Act which would change the absolute prohibition, which exists at present on mail opening in this country, of first-class mail in the first case. At present it is quite clear that first-class mail cannot be opened under any circumstances in this country and it is an indictable offence if it is done. In the bill put forward by the Postmaster General (Mr. Ouellet), we see that that fundamental principle has been altered and there is now a section there which would permit mail to be opened when there is a lawful excuse, whatever that means. Even if that section is violated, no longer is it an indictable offence but only a summary conviction offence.
The commitment we were given by the Solicitor General not to take any action on this until, first, there was a report from the RCMP and, second, there was a report from the McDonald commission, has indeed been violated, and 1 call upon the Solicitor General to urge his colleague, the Postmaster General, to withdraw that section, at least until such time as the evidence upon which it is based is forthcoming.
I should like to conclude by urging that before action is taken to justify this violation of the rights of privacy of
Canadians-one of the most fundamental and precious rights in terms of first-class mail-much more evidence be provided.
I would note, of course, that the Conservative party has been quick to sanction this violation of privacy. The Conservative party supported the concept of mail opening by the RCMP in 1979 by voting in favour of Bill C-26. Finally, 1 would note that the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Fraser) appears to have had a welcome conversion from his earlier support of that bill.
I thank the House for listening and I hope that before any action is taken on this matter far more evidence will be proposed and put before Parliament than has been the case so far.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ron Irwin (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Justice and Minister of State for Social Development):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Social Development
speechtext:
As my
good friend knows, Mr. Speaker, the Right Hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), in answer to the hon. member's questioning, set out the criteria. He said:
I am sure the hon. member would not want the government to take action and prosecute somebody on partial evidence. We have always said that we would not comment on the evidence as it came out in a piecemeal fashion; that we were waiting for the whole report. That remains our position.
The hon. member had asked if prosecutions were laid. He asked:
What action does the government intend to take to prosecute those persons who have been shown clearly to have violated the Post Office Act.
We spent over $11 million on the McDonald report. I know it is quite fashionable these days to pick out excerpts from the report and bring them before the House, but I do not consider that responsible. I respectfully submit that we should wait, especially in view of the fact that our police force wants to protect us, until all evidence is in to ascertain what should be done. From month to month we hear excerpts from the McDonald commission and from month to month we provide the same answer: Let us wait until we have the report. The Solicitor General has stated that he hopes the report will be in by early 1981, but we have been told that this might not be possible. At present, the Post Office legislation prohibits the opening of mail by anyone except in the presence of the addressee or for limited purposes. Evidence was produced at the McDonald commission hearings that this was being done illegally by members of the RCMP in spite of that legislation, and that was one of the major considerations for the establishment of the McDonald commission,
The Solicitor General has indicated to the commission, and they have agreed, that even if they are opposed to legislation which provides for mail opening, they should still make recommendations suggesting safeguards if Parliament should provide the necessary legislation. When we have received those recommendations, it is Parliament which will decide within which framework opening of mail will be or will not be permitted, and, if it is permitted, under what conditions.
It is a fine balance. If crimes are being committed through the mail, I suggest to the hon. member that it is incumbent
November 3, 1980

upon the RCMP to look at what is being done. For instance, heroin with a street value of $80,000 can be sent in an ordinary letter. I am not suggesting $80,000 worth of heroin is being sent, but I am suggesting that history has shown the mails are being used fraudulently and we can reasonably assume that the mails will be used fraudulently again. It is not only expected, it is incumbent upon the RCMP to find the balance between the privacy of an individual and the safeguard of the country. When the McDonald commission brings
Adjournment Debate
in its report, Parliament will decide. We can take apart the evidence as it comes in from the McDonald commission month by month, or I suggest we can do the responsible thing and wait until we get the report of the commission and then decide.

speechtext:

Tuesday, November 4, 1980
